cards.name: Recruitment ad / careers page copy
cards.summary: Job ads, EVP lines and careers-page copy that make the right people apply and the wrong ones self-select out. Good looks like the title candidates actually search for, a pay band, the first year described as outcomes, an honest trade-off, and an apply step that takes minutes, not an afternoon.
use_for: LinkedIn or Naukri job post for a hard-to-fill role
careers-page hero line plus 3-4 EVP (employee value proposition) pillars
campus or walk-in hiring notice for WhatsApp groups and college placement cells
hiring ads on LinkedIn or Meta that drive to an application form
rewriting a stale JD into a job ad that sells the role
avoid: Gender, age, marital or religion preferences ('male candidates only', 'below 30', 'unmarried preferred'): discriminatory, and in the US illegal in a job ad (EEOC). Describe the skill or condition the job needs instead ('comfortable with night shifts', 'two-wheeler and licence').
A 20-item requirements list: strong candidates who miss two items do not apply. Split 3-5 must-haves from 2-3 good-to-haves.
'Competitive salary' and 'fast-paced, dynamic environment': empty. Give the CTC band in LPA and one concrete fact about pace ('we ship to production twice a week').
Use genre:job_description when the client needs the internal document of record (grade, reporting line, KRAs) rather than a piece that sells the role.

recruitment agencies and RPO firms writing ads for clients
employer-branding and recruitment-marketing agencies
founders hiring their first 10-20 people
cards.value_why: Fiverr runs a job description writing subcategory and recruitment-copy agencies sell job ads, EVP statements and career sites as a line of work. Usually bought as a bundle (ad + careers page + social posts) or as part of an employer-brand project.
cards.goal: The right candidate applies through the stated channel after one read, and clearly unsuitable candidates decide not to.

structure.does: The standard title candidates search for, then city, work mode (on-site / hybrid / remote) and the CTC band. No 'ninja', no internal grade codes.
The problem the hire will own and why the company is hiring for it now (new plant, new market, a team that doubled).
Outcomes with a time frame, not duties: 'By month 6 you own the Meta budget of Rs 40 lakh a month'.
Must-haves as skills or proof of work, separated from good-to-haves. Years of experience only where they truly matter.
Pay band, specific benefits (health cover amount, leave days, learning budget) and one honest trade-off ('early-stage: processes are thin').
Who the company is in two or three sentences with one proof (customers, team size, funding, growth) and what working there is like, shown by a fact.
The exact step, how long it takes, what happens next and when, plus an equal-opportunity line.

length.note: A job ad on LinkedIn or Naukri sits at 250-500 words; senior or technical roles run longer; a careers-page EVP block or a WhatsApp campus notice is far shorter (60-150 words).

checklist: Is the title a standard, searchable job title with no slang ('rockstar', 'ninja', 'guru')?
Are city and work mode (on-site, hybrid, remote) stated?
Is a pay band given (or, if the client refuses, does the ad say when pay will be shared)?
Are responsibilities written as outcomes with a time frame rather than a list of duties?
Are must-haves (5 or fewer) separated from good-to-haves?
Is the ad free of gender, age, marital-status, religion or caste preferences?
Is every benefit specific (an amount, a number of days, a named policy)?
Does the ad name one honest trade-off or challenge of the role?
Does the apply section give the exact step, the time it takes and what happens next?
Can a candidate read it on a phone without hitting a wall of text?
pitfalls: Pasting the internal JD (KRAs, grade, reporting matrix) as the ad. The ad sells; lead with the problem the hire owns and keep the admin for the offer stage.
'Freshers with 2-3 years of experience' and other contradictions from merged templates. Read the requirements as a candidate would.
'Immediate joiners only' with no reason: signals churn and shrinks the pool. If speed matters, say why and whether you buy out notice periods.
AI-sounding EVP ('We are a passionate, dynamic family'): replace each adjective with a fact ('11 of our 40 people were promoted internally last year').
Hiding the salary: Indian candidates filter by CTC and recruiters field the same question 50 times. Give a band in LPA.
Collecting Aadhaar, PAN or photos at the application stage: unnecessary personal data. Ask for them at offer stage only.
cards.exemplar_brief: LinkedIn job ad (also used on the careers page) for a Senior Performance Marketing Manager at a fictional Pune D2C skincare brand ('Kesar & Co', 60 people, Series A); audience: performance marketers with 5-8 years' experience, now at agencies in Pune or Mumbai; offer: Rs 28-34 LPA, hybrid with 3 days a week in the Baner office, owns a Rs 40 lakh monthly Meta and Google budget; English (Indian); 300-450 words; goal: qualified applications through a 3-question form.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Every part present and in order: searchable title with city, hybrid 3-days-Baner and Rs 28-34 LPA; why-now tied to the Rs 40 lakh Meta/Google budget; outcomes on a month 1/3/6/9 clock; must-haves as proof of work; honest trade-off ('processes are thin'); 3-question form with time to complete, reply window and next step; equal-opportunity line. Benefits/proof are visible placeholders (brief gave none). Nits: only one good-to-have (card asks 2-3) and 'By month 3' used twice; About-us could carry one more concrete fact than '60 people, Series A'.

cards.name: Reddit post (organic community post)
cards.summary: A text post written as a member of one subreddit: a plain, specific title, a body that hands over the useful thing in full (numbers, steps, what went wrong), affiliation disclosed up front, and one question that invites comments. Good looks like a post that would still be upvoted if the brand name were deleted.
use_for: founder or engineer sharing a lessons-learned or numbers post in a relevant subreddit
asking a community for honest feedback on a product, with affiliation disclosed
ghostwriting a post for an expert who will post and answer comments from their own account
announcing an AMA in a subreddit that allows them
sharing original data or a how-to that answers a question the subreddit keeps asking
avoid: Posting as a 'happy customer' or a fake persona: astroturfing breaks subreddit rules, gets the account banned and becomes the story. Post as who you are and say it.
A promotional post with the link in line one: removed by mods or downvoted. Give the full value in the post; put a link only where the subreddit's rules allow (often in a comment, on request).
Copy-pasting one post into ten subreddits: each community has its own rules, flair and in-jokes. Rewrite the title and opening per subreddit or pick the one best fit.
Use genre:quora_answer when you are answering someone else's question, genre:community_post for a brand-owned community, and genre:comment_reply for replies in a thread.

sources.title: Fiverr: Social Media Copywriting category (Platform facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Reddit is a platform filter in Fiverr social media copywriting, 96 gigs on 2026-10-04 (supply signal, small)

buyers: founders and dev-tools or SaaS teams doing community-led growth
agencies running Reddit and forum seeding for brands (disclosed)
experts, authors and creators who want posts written for their own accounts
consumer brands preparing an AMA
cards.value_why: Fiverr's social media copywriting category lists Reddit as a platform with only 96 gigs on 2026-10-04, a small supply signal. Brand interest is growing because Reddit threads surface in Google and AI answers (see trend:reddit_and_forums_in_search), but most of the work is the account owner's own voice and replies.
cards.goal: Members of the subreddit upvote the post and reply with their own experience or questions, without mods removing it.

structure.does: Read the subreddit's rules, pinned posts, flair options and the top posts of the past month. Decide if the post is allowed at all and which flair it needs.
Says exactly what is inside, in plain words, with the specific number or situation. No clickbait, no ALL CAPS, no emoji.
structure.length: under 120 characters is typical; hard cap in plat:reddit_post

structure.does: One line on who is posting and any affiliation ('I run X, so I am biased'), plus a TL;DR for long posts.
The full story, data or steps: what you tried, the numbers, what failed and what you would do differently. Uses Reddit markdown (short headers, lists) sparingly.
One specific question to the community ('Has anyone moved Postgres off RDS at under 50 GB? What broke?'). No sales CTA.
Prepared answers to the 3 likely objections and the links you will share only if asked; the poster replies within the first hours.

length.note: A discussion question can be 60-120 words; a lessons or data post runs 400-900 with a TL;DR. The subreddit's top posts set the real norm.

checklist: Does the title say what the post contains, with a specific number or situation?
If a brand or product is involved, is the affiliation stated in the first three lines?
Does the post deliver its full value without the reader clicking any link?
Is the body free of marketing adjectives and slogans?
Does it include at least one detail only someone who did the thing would know?
Does a post over 300 words open with a TL;DR?
Does it end with one specific question rather than a sales call to action?
Is there no link in the body, unless the subreddit's rules allow it?
Does it match the subreddit's stated format and flair rules?
pitfalls: Opening with 'Hey Reddit!' or a brand intro. Open with the situation: 'We spent Rs 3 lakh on Google Ads for a B2B tool and got 4 demos. Here is the breakdown.'
Press-release voice ('We are thrilled to announce'): reads as an ad and gets downvoted. Write as one tired, honest practitioner talking to peers.
Bulleted, bolded, emoji-headed 'listicle' bodies that look machine-made. Use plain paragraphs with one short list where it helps.
Arguing with critics in comments. Thank, concede what is fair, add data; never ask friends to upvote (vote manipulation).
Deleting and reposting a post that underperformed: mods notice. Learn, then post something new another week.
Hinglish in a global subreddit, or stiff English in an Indian one where the top posts are casual Hinglish. Mirror the community.

cards.exemplar_brief: r/developersIndia text post from the CTO of a fictional Bengaluru dev-tools startup ('LogLantern', an open-source log viewer) on how the team cut its AWS bill from Rs 4.2 lakh to Rs 1.6 lakh a month in 10 weeks, including one change that backfired; audience: Indian backend engineers; affiliation disclosed, no link in the body; English (Indian, casual); 400-600 words with a TL;DR; goal: upvotes and comments that share their own cost cuts or ask for the repo.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2-. Title states the number and the twist; disclosure + no-link line in the first 3 lines; TL;DR; practitioner detail only someone who did it knows (NAT charges hiding under EC2-Other, free S3 gateway endpoint, Glacier Flexible Retrieval 90-day minimum and retrieval fees, Standard-IA 30-day rule: all correct AWS behaviour); backfire told honestly; ends on a specific community question. Per-item savings are [saving: Rs X] placeholders (brief gave only the totals). Nit: 'the Rs 2.6 lakh a month we lost from the bill' should be 'cut from'.

cards.name: Release notes / changelog
cards.summary: A per-version record of what changed, written for the people who use the product. Good looks like a version and date on top, breaking changes and the steps to handle them first, then changes grouped by type, each line saying what the user can now do or no longer needs to worry about, in the words the UI uses.
use_for: SaaS changelog page or in-app 'What's new' panel
App Store and Play Store 'What's new' text
CHANGELOG.md for an open-source library or API
release email to admins when a change needs action
internal release notes for support and sales teams
avoid: Dumping ticket titles ('FE-2231 fix modal z-index'): users cannot tell what changed for them. Rewrite each as user impact: 'The invoice preview no longer hides behind the sidebar on small laptops.'
Only 'Bug fixes and performance improvements' every release: tells nobody anything and hides real changes. Name at least the fixes users reported.
Hype ('revolutionary new dashboard') in a changelog: users read it for facts. Put the launch story in genre:product_update_newsletter and link to it.
Use genre:readme for project setup docs, genre:knowledge_base_article for how-to help, and genre:api_reference for endpoint details.

mobile app teams shipping store updates

cards.value_why: A routine product-team deliverable, usually owned by technical writers or product marketing and rarely commissioned alone. Technical writing pays above general writing: BLS median $90,390 (May 2025) and AmbitionBox India average Rs 8.5 lakh a year, about double a content writer.
cards.goal: A user learns in under a minute what changed for them and does any required action (update, migrate, re-check a setting) before it bites.

structure.does: Version number and release date in an unambiguous format (2026-10-04 or 4 October 2026); optional short release name.
The one to three changes most users care about, each as what the user can now do.
What breaks, who is affected, the exact steps to adapt and any deadline. Always above the other groups when present.
Items under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security; one line each, user impact first, link to docs or issue where useful.
Open problems and the workaround, so support does not field the same ticket 100 times.
Docs for new features, full diff or migration guide, where to send feedback.

length.note: A patch release is a few lines; a major release with migrations runs long and links a separate migration guide. Store 'What's new' fields have character caps (see plat:apple_app_store).

checklist: Does each release show a version number and a date?
Is the newest release at the top?
If anything breaks, is it listed before all other changes, with steps to adapt?
Does every line describe the effect on the user rather than an internal ticket title?
Are changes grouped under consistent headings (Added, Changed, Fixed and so on)?
Are feature and setting names spelled exactly as they appear in the UI?
Are security fixes flagged as security fixes?
Does every new feature line link to docs or say where to find it?
Is the text free of marketing adjectives?
pitfalls: Internal codenames and component names ('Phoenix v2', 'the ledger service'). Use the label the user clicks.
Ambiguous dates like 04/10/2026, which Indian and US readers read differently. Use 2026-10-04 or 4 October 2026.
Deprecations hidden under 'Changed'. Give them their own heading with the removal date.
Passive lines that hide who must act ('Templates should be updated'). Say 'If you use a custom invoice template, update it before 31 October.'
Copy-pasting the same store 'What's new' text every release; users stop reading. Name one real change each time.
Jokes and emoji in a changelog for finance, health or admin users; save personality for consumer apps that already use it.
cards.exemplar_brief: Release notes for version 4.2.0 of a fictional Chennai-built GST billing SaaS ('BillBook Pro') used by wholesale distributors. DEMO DATA: every fact below is invented for this test assignment; use these facts and no others. Release date: 6 October 2026. (1) Added: bulk e-invoice upload; users upload one Excel file of up to 500 invoices under Billing > E-invoice > Bulk upload instead of one at a time. (2) Changed, action required: the default rounding rule changes from rounding each invoice line to 2 decimals to rounding the invoice total to the nearest rupee; custom invoice templates that print line amounts will no longer add up to the printed total, so users must update them under Settings > Templates > Round-off before 31 October 2026; the standard templates update automatically. (3) Fixed: the invoice preview no longer hides behind the sidebar on laptops narrower than 1366 pixels; the GSTR-1 export no longer drops invoices dated the 31st of a month; the customer ledger PDF no longer shows the previous month's closing balance on page 2. (4) Security: a password-reset link could be reused after a successful reset; each link now works once; no action needed and no sign of misuse. Known issue: bulk upload rejects files over 5 MB (workaround: split the file). Write the changelog entry in plain English for non-native readers on the changelog page, plus a 2-line Play Store 'What's new' version; 150-300 words; goal: affected users update their templates before 31 October 2026.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Structure is right: version header, highlights, 'Action required before 31 October 2026' above the grouped changes with who is affected and numbered steps, Added/Changed/Fixed/Security, links, plus a clean 2-line Play Store version. But most user-impact lines are brackets ([old rule], [new rule], 3 fixes, the security line, release date), so the sample cannot show the card's core skill of ticket-to-impact rewriting; Known issues omitted. 'If you use only the standard templates, you do nothing' reads non-native. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> state the old and new rounding rule (e.g. 'per-line rounding to 2 decimals changes to rounding the invoice total to the nearest rupee'), the release date, and one line each for the 3 bug fixes and the security fix. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): exemplar_brief now states old/new rounding rule, release date, 3 fixes, security fix, known issue (demo data); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Repurposed content (video/podcast to blog, thread, carousel)
cards.summary: A set of new pieces cut from one source asset (podcast, webinar, video, talk, long report), each rebuilt with its own hook, structure and format for its platform. Good looks like outputs that each stand alone, carry the source's sharpest specifics with quotes checked word for word, credit the speaker and point back to the original.
use_for: podcast episode into a blog post, a LinkedIn carousel and 2-3 reel scripts
webinar into a recap email, an X thread and a short how-to article
founder keynote or YouTube video into a week of LinkedIn posts
long research report into WhatsApp channel posts and carousels
Hinglish video into English blog plus Hinglish shorts for a two-audience brand
avoid: A cleaned-up transcript posted as a blog: rambling, chronological, no hook. Rebuild the piece around one reader question and pull the best answers into it.
One caption pasted across Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube: each platform reads differently and some demote reposts (trend:original_content_ranking). Write each output for its home.
Paraphrase drift: a guest's 'can help in some cases' becomes 'guarantees results'. Quote from the transcript, and get the guest's OK on any claim about money or health.
Use genre:podcast_show_notes when the client only needs the episode page, and genre:content_refresh when updating an old article rather than making new pieces.

sources.title: Fiverr: Podcast Writing category (Service includes facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: podcast-writing gigs sell deliverables derived from recordings: episode summary, segment timestamps, show notes, script writing (gig counts, supply signal)

buyers: podcasters and YouTubers who want a written and short-video footprint
B2B marketing teams running webinars and founder talks
social media agencies on monthly retainers
coaches and creators turning courses or lives into posts
cards.value_why: Fiverr podcast-writing gigs already sell summaries, show notes and timestamps derived from recordings (2026-10-04), and repurposing is commonly bundled into social retainers. Rarely bought alone; it is a volume line inside a retainer.
cards.goal: Each output earns attention on its own platform and sends a share of readers back to the full source.

structure.does: From the transcript, list 5-10 moments worth reusing (a number, a story, a contrarian claim, a how-to), each with the exact quote and timestamp.
Assign moments to outputs: platform, hook, the one idea, the CTA back to the source. One idea per short piece; no moment used twice in the same week.
Blog post or newsletter organised around a reader's question, not the episode's order; descriptive subheads; quotes attributed by name.
Carousel, reel or short script, thread or LinkedIn post, each with its own native hook and format.
structure.length: per format: carousel 6-10 slides, reel 30-60 seconds, thread 5-8 posts, post 120-250 words

structure.does: Name the speaker or guest and point to the full episode (link, episode number or timestamp) in every output.
Every quote and number checked against the transcript; every piece read once without the source to confirm it stands alone.

length.note: Whole package; driven by how many outputs the client buys. Each output follows its own genre card for length (genre:carousel_copy, genre:short_form_video_script, genre:blog_post).

checklist: Does each output open with its own hook rather than 'In this episode'?
Does each short output carry exactly one idea?
Does each piece make sense to someone who has not heard the source?
Does every quote match the transcript word for word (or is clearly marked as a paraphrase)?
Is the speaker or guest credited by name in every output?
Does every output point back to the full source?
Do no two outputs share the same opening line?
Is the long piece organised by the reader's question rather than the episode's running order?
Is the text free of transcript leftovers (ums, 'as I said earlier', speaker labels)?
pitfalls: Chronological recaps ('First we talked about..., then...'). Lead with the single most useful answer and build the piece around it.
Translating a Hinglish source line by line into stiff English. Transcreate: keep the idea and the punch, rewrite the sentence.
Lifting a number without its condition ('saved 40%' when the guest said 'in our pilot of 12 stores'). Carry the condition along with the number.
Ten outputs from one weak episode. If the source has three good moments, make three pieces.
Reusing the same clip and caption across platforms and accounts; rework the hook and the opening frame for each.
Repurposing someone else's podcast or video without permission beyond fair-dealing limits; get the owner's OK or quote briefly with credit.
cards.exemplar_brief: Repurpose a 52-minute Hinglish episode of a fictional Mumbai personal-finance podcast ('Paisa Pe Charcha') in which a SEBI-registered adviser explains why a 30-year-old should buy term insurance instead of a ULIP: one 900-word English blog post, one 8-slide Hinglish Instagram carousel and two 45-second Hinglish reel scripts, each with its own hook, the adviser credited and a pointer to the full episode; goal: new listeners for the episode.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2-. Output plan, ~900-word English blog organised around the reader's question ('ULIP or term at 30?') not episode order, 8-slide Hinglish carousel and two 45-s Hinglish reels with distinct hooks, adviser credited and episode pointer in every output, quote-check note. ULIP facts are right (5-year lock-in; allocation, admin, mortality, fund-management charges; tax rules changed and are hedged). Adviser quotes are [exact quote, mm:ss] slots because no transcript was supplied: correct handling, not invention. Nits: carousel slide 1 promises '5 baatein' but the slides do not number five; Reel B CTA repeats 'Poora'.

cards.name: Research abstract
cards.summary: The short structured summary (background, methods, results, conclusion) that reviewers and database readers use to decide whether to read or accept a study. Good looks like one sentence of gap and aim, methods with design and sample size, the main result as a number with its uncertainty, and a conclusion that claims no more than the data shows, inside the venue's word limit and headings.
use_for: journal submission abstract (structured or unstructured)
conference abstract submission
thesis or dissertation abstract
poster abstract and the summary for a preprint server
editing a non-native author's abstract into clear English
avoid: Half the words on background: reviewers want the result. One or two sentences of context, then aim, methods, results.
'Significant improvement was observed' with no number: report the effect, its size and its uncertainty ('HbA1c fell 0.6 points, 95% CI 0.3-0.9').
A conclusion that goes beyond the study ('this will transform rural healthcare'). Conclude what this sample and design support, then one line on what to test next.
Use genre:thesis_summary for a lay or plain-language summary, and genre:executive_summary for a business audience.

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Research Summaries
sources.supports: research-summary category exists on the Writing & Translation menu

buyers: researchers, PhD scholars and medical residents
academic and medical editing services
pharma and medical-communications agencies preparing congress abstracts
research teams at think tanks and NGOs
cards.value_why: Usually written by the researchers themselves; paid help comes through research-summary and academic-editing services (Fiverr runs a Research Summaries category). Medical-communications abstracts pay better but sit inside larger projects.
cards.goal: A reviewer or reader understands the question, the method and the main result in one read and decides to accept or read the full paper.

structure.does: Names the population, exposure or intervention, outcome and design ('...: a cross-sectional study').
The gap in one sentence and the aim or hypothesis in one sentence.
Design, setting, period, participants and n, intervention or exposure, primary outcome, main analysis.
Primary outcome first with numbers, effect size and confidence interval or test; then one or two key secondary results.
What the result means for this population, the main limitation if critical, and the next step. No new data.
Terms the venue asks for, chosen for indexing.

length.note: Each journal or conference sets its own word limit and headings; read the author guidelines first and write to that exact limit.

checklist: Is it within the venue's word limit?
Does it use the venue's headings in the venue's order?
Is the aim stated in one sentence?
Do the methods give design, setting, period and sample size?
Is the primary result reported as a number with an effect size, interval or test?
Is every abbreviation defined at first use (or avoided)?
Does the conclusion stay within what the results show?
Does every number match the full paper's tables?
Is it free of citations and of 'will be discussed' promises?
pitfalls: Writing the abstract before analysis and never updating it: numbers drift from the tables. Rewrite it last and check each number against the results.
'Results will be presented at the conference': reviewers reject abstracts without results. If data is incomplete, give interim numbers and say so.
p-values with no effect size ('p<0.05'). Give the difference and the interval first, p second.
Hype words ('novel', 'first-ever', 'groundbreaking') that reviewers discount. Let the result carry the weight.
Indian academic filler ('It is pertinent to mention that'). Cut to the claim.
Different terms for the same thing (respondents, participants, subjects). Pick one and keep it.

ban.label: promise instead of result, or hype

cards.exemplar_brief: Structured conference abstract (Background, Methods, Results, Conclusions) for a fictional cross-sectional study from a Jaipur government medical college: anaemia prevalence among 412 adolescent girls in 6 rural schools and its association with drinking tea with meals; audience: reviewers of a national public-health conference; English; at most 250 words; goal: accepted for oral presentation. DEMO DATA: the study and every figure are invented for this test assignment; report these figures and no others. Study period January-March 2026; ages 13-17 years (mean 15.1); anaemia = haemoglobin below 12.0 g/dL. Prevalence 52.9% (218 of 412; 95% CI 48.1-57.7). Tea with meals (within an hour of a main meal, 4 or more days a week): 183 girls, of whom 62.8% (115) were anaemic, against 45.0% (103 of 229) of the rest (chi-square p < 0.001). Adjusted OR for anaemia with tea with meals: 1.8 (95% CI 1.2-2.7), from logistic regression adjusted for age, family size and weekly leafy-vegetable intake. Secondary result: girls who took weekly iron-folic acid tablets regularly (241 girls) had anaemia in 44.8% (108), against 64.3% (110 of 171) of the others.

verified.note: P1 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. Venue headings in order, title names population/exposure/design, aim in one sentence, methods name design, setting and n = 412, analysis plan (chi-square + adjusted logistic regression), conclusion stays inside a cross-sectional design and names a next step; 245 words, no citations. But every result (prevalence, CI, adjusted OR, p) is a bracket, and the card itself says reviewers reject abstracts without results, so the piece cannot be judged on the card's central checklist item; 'higher odds' presumes the direction. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply the results to report (study period, age range, prevalence with 95% CI, adjusted OR with CI for tea with meals, one secondary result), or state 'invent and label illustrative figures' for this fictional study. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): exemplar_brief now supplies study period, ages, prevalence+CI, adjusted OR+CI, secondary result (demo data); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Data-driven / original research post
cards.summary: An article built on numbers nobody else has (a survey, a scrape, anonymised product data), written so journalists, creators and AI answers can cite a single sentence. Good looks like the headline finding in the title, a methodology box, three to seven findings each with a chart and a one-line takeaway, and implications the reader can act on.
use_for: SaaS or marketplace publishing anonymised platform data ('what 18,000 job posts tell us')
customer or industry survey write-up
public-data or scraped-data study (prices, reviews, listings)
blog version of a gated research report
link-earning and digital PR campaigns
avoid: A thin sample presented as industry truth (37 responses called 'Indian marketers think'). Call it a pulse poll, state n, or collect more data first.
Burying the method at the bottom or leaving it out: journalists will not cite it. Put a methodology box near the top.
Chart dumps with no takeaway. Every chart needs a one-sentence caption saying what it shows.
Use genre:research_report for the long gated version and genre:informational_article when there is no original data.

cards.value_why: Fiverr lists 'Research article' as its own article type (1713 gigs on 2026-10-04) and article gigs sell 'Data chart' add-ons. Pays above a standard blog post because it needs analysis and charts, but the data usually comes from the client's analyst.
cards.goal: Readers, journalists and AI answers quote at least one finding and credit the publisher, and target readers act on the implications.

structure.does: States the main finding with its number ('Tier-2 cities fill warehouse jobs 9 days faster than metros').
Two-line summary, then 3-5 bullet findings, each a quotable sentence with a number and its base.
Source of data, sample size, period, how collected, how cleaned, limits. Sponsor named if any.
One section per finding: the finding as the subhead, one chart, what it shows, why it might be so (labelled as interpretation), what it means.
What a reader in the target role should do differently, tied to specific findings.
How to cite, link to data or full report, contact for press.

length.note: Driven by the number of findings worth a chart; better five strong findings than twelve weak ones.

checklist: Does the headline contain the main finding and its number?
Does a methodology box give data source, sample size, period and collection method?
Does every percentage have its base (n) stated nearby?
Does every chart have a one-sentence takeaway caption?
Is each finding's subhead a full sentence stating the finding?
Are interpretations labelled as such, with no causal claims the data cannot support?
Are limitations stated?
Are number formats consistent (lakh/crore or million, not both)?
Can at least three findings be quoted on their own?
Is there a clear way to cite or download the data?
pitfalls: 'Studies show' when it is your own study. Say 'Our analysis of 18,400 applications shows'.
Percentages of tiny subgroups ('62% of Kochi respondents' when n=13). Merge groups or drop the cut.
Causal language from a survey ('remote work causes burnout'). Write 'is associated with' and offer a reason as a hypothesis.
Rounding that does not add up (49.6% in the chart, 'half' in text, 51% in the summary). Fix one number and use it everywhere.
Hiding the sponsor or the sponsor's product in the findings; disclose and keep product mentions out of the findings sections.
Personal data in examples or screenshots; aggregate and anonymise everything shown.
cards.exemplar_brief: Blog post for a fictional Bengaluru HR-tech SaaS ('ShiftSathi') publishing anonymised data from 18,400 blue-collar job applications on its platform (January-June 2026): which cities, shifts and pay bands get roles filled fastest; audience: HR heads at logistics and retail companies; English (Indian); 1,200-1,600 words with a methodology box and 4 chart captions; goal: journalists and LinkedIn creators cite a stat and readers download the full report. DEMO DATA: the dataset and every figure are invented for this test assignment; use these figures and no others. Base: the 18,400 applications went to 2,240 roles; 1,980 were filled within 60 days and are the base for every time-to-fill median (days from posting to the employer marking the role filled). Metros = Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune; 14 other cities = Tier-2. Findings: (1) Tier-2 roles filled in a median 6 days vs 11 in metros (n = 1,140 vs 840 roles). (2) Night-shift roles took a median 10 days vs 6 for day shifts, 4 days slower (n = 412 vs 1,568 roles). (3) The Rs 18,000-22,000 monthly pay band filled in a median 7 days vs 12 for the Rs 14,000-18,000 band, 5 days faster (n = 724 vs 802 roles). (4) 13,064 of the 18,400 applications (71%) came through the WhatsApp apply link; 5,336 (29%) used the web form. Limits: only roles posted on the platform; employers mark 'filled' themselves; January-June may be seasonal.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Uses only the supplied demo figures and they reconcile (1,140 + 840 and 412 + 1,568 = 1,980 filled roles; 260 excluded; 71% = 13,064 of 18,400). A finding-and-number headline, a standfirst and four quotable bullets with bases, a methodology box near the top that states the 60-day cut and its bias, four finding subheads with chart captions, labelled interpretations with no causal claims, a 'what these numbers do not tell you' section, five implications tied to findings, cite and download. Nit (writer): the chart captions restate the subheads. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Research paper / thesis section
cards.summary: One section of a journal manuscript or thesis written to the venue's format. Good looks like an Introduction that narrows from field to gap to aim, Methods another team could repeat, Results that report without interpreting, and a Discussion that opens with the main finding, compares it with prior work and admits its limits, with every claim cited and every number matching the tables.
use_for: restructuring and editing a researcher's draft Introduction or Discussion
turning lab notes and protocols into a Methods section
writing Results text from an analyst's tables
language editing for non-native authors submitting to international journals
restructuring a thesis chapter to the university's format
avoid: Ghostwriting assessed work (a student's thesis or coursework): marketplaces and universities bar it. Offer editing, structure feedback or coaching on the student's own draft instead.
Interpreting inside Results ('this suggests that...'). Report there; interpret in the Discussion.
An Introduction that is a literature dump. Cite only what builds the path to the gap and the aim; use genre:literature_review for a standalone review.
Use genre:research_abstract for the abstract and genre:thesis_summary for a lay summary.

buyers: researchers and faculty preparing manuscripts
academic and medical editing firms
pharma and medical-communications agencies (with named authors)

cards.value_why: Paid academic and medical editing exist, but ghostwriting assessed work is barred by marketplaces and universities (Upwork policy). The legitimate market is editing, restructuring and medical writing for named authors.
cards.goal: Reviewers find the section complete, correctly formatted and supported by evidence, so they judge the science rather than the writing.

structure.does: Field and why it matters, what is known (cited), the specific gap, and in the last paragraph the aim or hypothesis.
Design, setting and dates, participants or materials, procedures, outcomes and how measured, statistical analysis, ethics approval and consent. Subheaded so it can be checked.
Findings in the same order as the methods, numbers with uncertainty, tables and figures cited in text; no interpretation, no citations.
structure.length: text that leads the reader through the tables, not repeats them

structure.does: Principal finding in the first paragraph, comparison with named prior studies, possible explanations, strengths and limitations, implications, and a short conclusion.

length.note: Per section; the journal's total word limit and the thesis format decide the split. Methods length is set by what replication needs, not by a target.

checklist: Does the section use the journal's or university's required headings?
Does the Introduction end with an explicit aim or hypothesis?
Does every factual claim in the Introduction and Discussion carry a citation?
Do the Methods give enough detail (n, setting, dates, instruments, tests, software) to repeat the study?
Is ethics approval or consent stated where people or animals were involved?
Are the Results free of interpretation and citations?
Does every number in the text match the tables and figures?
Does the Discussion open with the principal finding?
Are limitations stated plainly?
Are terms and abbreviations used consistently throughout?
pitfalls: Tense mix-ups. Methods and Results in past tense ('we measured'); established knowledge in present ('anaemia impairs').
Filler common in Indian academic drafts ('It is pertinent to mention', 'Needless to say'). Delete and state the claim.
Repeating every table value in the text. Point to the table and pull out only the two or three numbers that matter.
A Discussion that re-reads the Results. Interpret: compare, explain, qualify.
Copying Methods text from the authors' earlier paper: plagiarism checkers flag it and Indian universities run them on theses. Rewrite or cite the earlier protocol.
Overclaiming from one study ('proves', 'confirms') in a field paper. Use 'shows', 'is consistent with', and name what would confirm it.

ban.label: academic filler

cards.exemplar_brief: Discussion section for a fictional paper from a Pune agricultural university: a two-season field trial in Maharashtra in which drip irrigation with plastic mulch raised onion yield by 18% and cut water use by 31% compared with furrow irrigation; audience: reviewers at an international agronomy journal; English (UK); 900-1,200 words; must open with the principal finding, compare with three prior studies (marked [ref]) and state three limitations; goal: reviewers accept the claims as supported.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. Opens with the principal finding (yield +18%, water -31%), derives water productivity correctly (1.18/0.69 = about 1.7), mechanisms hedged and cited [ref] (onion shallow-rooted and weak competitor, mulch on evaporation/weeds/soil temperature: sound agronomy), three prior-study comparisons, season interaction, three plain limitations including the drip/mulch confound, strengths, implications, next steps; UK spelling, past tense for results, no 'proves'. The three comparisons are bracket shells because no studies were supplied; acceptable under the brief's '[ref]' instruction. 925 words, inside 900-1,200.

cards.name: Research / state-of report
cards.summary: A designed report that publishes original survey or usage data ('State of X 2026'), used for PR, links, sales conversations and leads. Good looks like one big story told by the data, an executive summary that stands alone, a transparent methodology, findings chapters with charts and quotable lines, and recommendations tied to specific findings.
use_for: annual 'State of' report for a SaaS, fintech or agency
industry benchmark report (pay, pricing, adoption, performance)
association or chamber member survey report
anchor asset for a PR and link campaign
gated lead magnet and sales-conversation data
avoid: Sixty charts and no story. Pick the three to five findings that change what the reader does and build chapters around them.
Writing before seeing the tables: you will build a narrative the data does not support. Ask the analyst for crosstabs and bases first.
A sponsor's product inside the findings: readers and journalists stop trusting the numbers. Keep the product to a clearly marked page.
Use genre:research_article for the blog version, genre:white_paper for an argued paper without original data, and genre:ebook_lead_magnet for a how-to guide.

structure.does: Title names the report; subtitle states the headline finding.
Five to seven key findings, each a sentence with a number, plus a one-line implication each. Readable without the rest.
Who was asked or measured, n, fieldwork dates, how recruited, any weighting, margin of error if applicable, sponsor, limits.
Three to six chapters, each headed by a finding sentence, with charts, commentary, segment cuts and a pull-quote or expert comment.
How results differ by company size, city tier, role or sector, shown only where the base is big enough.
Five to seven actions, each tied to a named finding.
Publisher, questionnaire or data definitions, respondent profile.

checklist: Can the executive summary be read alone and still give the main findings with numbers?
Does the methodology state who, how many, when, how recruited and the limits?
Is each chapter headed by a finding sentence rather than a topic label?
Does every chart show a title, the base (n) and a takeaway?
Is every recommendation tied to a specific finding?
Are segment comparisons shown only where the base is stated and adequate?
Is the sponsor disclosed?
Are percentage-point and percent changes used correctly?
Are there at least five findings a journalist could quote on their own?

pitfalls: An executive summary that reads like a table of contents ('Chapter 2 explores...'). Write findings, not chapter descriptions.
Year-on-year comparisons when the question wording or sample changed. Flag the change or drop the comparison.
Generalising 'respondents' to 'Indians' or 'all MSMEs'. Say who the sample is every time it matters.
Confusing percentage points with percent ('UPI use rose 20%' when it went from 40% to 60%, a 20-point rise).

cards.exemplar_brief: Executive summary and methodology (the first four pages) of a fictional 'State of MSME Digital Payments 2026' report by a Jaipur fintech ('KhataPay'), based on a survey of 2,150 MSME owners across 14 Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities (fieldwork July-August 2026); audience: bank product heads, journalists and policy staff; English (Indian); 900-1,200 words; goal: readers download the full PDF and journalists quote two findings. DEMO DATA: the survey and every figure are invented for this test assignment; use these figures and no others. Method: phone interviews with 2,150 owners (1,230 in 8 Tier-2 cities, 920 in 6 Tier-3 cities); recruited from KhataPay's merchant list and bank-partner referrals, so a non-probability sample: no weighting and no margin of error claimed; answers self-reported; businesses without a phone excluded; KhataPay publishes and sponsors the report. Findings: (1) 71% of owners accept UPI at the counter (1,521 of 2,150). (2) Acceptance is 78% in Tier-2 cities (960 of 1,230) vs 61% in Tier-3 (561 of 920), a gap of 17 percentage points. (3) Among the 1,521 accepting owners, digital payments average 46% of monthly sales value. (4) 64% of all 2,150 owners pay most supplier invoices in cash, 27% by bank transfer or UPI, 9% by cheque or other. (5) Of the 629 owners who do not accept UPI, 44% say customers pay cash anyway and 31% fear delayed settlement. (6) 9% of the 1,521 accepting owners have used a credit line or overdraft tied to their digital sales.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. The subtitle states the story (money arrives digitally and leaves in cash); six findings with bases and one-line implications, each quotable alone; a methodology of about 250 words naming the non-probability sample, no weighting or margin of error, self-report, exclusions and the sponsor, and warning that acceptance may run high; the pp-vs-percent rule; how to cite plus two quote-ready lines; all figures check (1,521/2,150 = 71%, 960/1,230 = 78%, 561/920 = 61%, 629 non-accepters). Nit (writer): 'a small share route most sales through it' goes beyond what an average of 46% shows. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Resignation letter
cards.summary: A brief formal letter or email that resigns, states the last working day under the notice period, thanks the employer and offers a handover. Good looks like the resignation in the first sentence, an exact date, no grievances, one specific thank-you and a concrete handover plan, in under 250 words.
use_for: standard resignation email to the reporting manager, copied to HR
resignation with a request for early release or notice buyout
resignation during probation
stepping down from a board, committee or volunteer role
formal printed letter where the employer requires one
avoid: Listing grievances: the letter goes into the personnel file and may be read by future reference checkers. Raise issues in the exit interview or a separate note to HR.
Negotiating a counter-offer in the letter. If you are open to staying, talk first; the letter is for a decision.
A vague last day ('in about two months'). Give the date and reference the notice clause.
Use genre:internal_announcement for the farewell note to the team, and genre:recommendation_letter when asking a manager for a reference.
buyers: individual employees (usually free templates; occasionally career coaches)
HR teams writing template libraries
resume and career-service writers bundling it
cards.value_why: Template-driven with no meaningful paid market; it shows up as a free extra in career-service bundles.
cards.goal: The manager and HR accept the resignation with the stated last working day, and the relationship stays good enough for a reference.

structure.does: Identifies the email: 'Resignation: [Full name], [Employee ID]'.
Resigns from the named role, with the date of the letter.
References the notice period in the contract and gives the exact last working day; any early-release or buyout request goes here with a reason.
One or two specific things the person is grateful for (a project, a skill, a manager's support).
What will be documented and handed over, to whom, by when.
Asks HR for the relieving letter and full-and-final settlement process, gives personal contact details, signs off.

length.note: Longer only when an early-release request or a complex handover needs explaining.

checklist: Does the first sentence state the resignation?
Are the role and the letter's date stated?
Is the last working day given as an exact date (day, month, year)?
Does the notice period referenced match the contract?
Is the letter free of complaints and blame?
Is the thank-you specific rather than generic?
Is the handover offer concrete (what, to whom, by when)?
Does it ask for the relieving letter and full-and-final settlement contact?
Is it under 250 words with no template placeholders left in?
pitfalls: Ambiguous dates (04/10/2026). Write '31 October 2026'.
Naming the new employer or the salary jump. Neither is required; both can sour the exit.
Resigning only on WhatsApp or by phone. Follow up in writing on official email so the date is on record.
Asking to skip the notice period with no handover plan. Offer the plan first, then the request.
Over-emotional or sarcastic thanks. One warm, specific sentence reads better.
Leaving '[Company Name]' or '[Manager]' from a template in the sent letter.
cards.exemplar_brief: Resignation email from a senior accountant at a fictional Indore pharma distributor ('Malwa Medisupply') to her manager, copied to HR, leaving after 4 years for a role in Pune; notice period 60 days under her contract, asking for release after 45 days with a full handover of GST filings and vendor reconciliations; English (Indian); 120-200 words; goal: the manager agrees to the early release and the relationship stays warm.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Subject in the card's format, resignation in sentence one, 60-day contract notice with exact dates that check out (6 Oct + 60 = 5 Dec 2026; + 45 = 20 Nov; 15 days), handover plan first and then the release request, buyout offer, relieving letter and F&F asked of HR, no new employer or pay named, ~190 words. Plan timing fits GST (GSTR-3B for October due 20 November). Nits: thanks sits after the handover rather than before; 'we will run the October filing together' then 'I will complete both for October myself' is muddled; 'I have learned a great deal here' is generic.

cards.name: Restaurant menu copy
cards.summary: Dish names, dish descriptions, section intros and the restaurant's story blurb that help a diner choose and make them want to. Good looks like names that say what the dish is, descriptions of 10-25 words with the main ingredient, the method and one sensory or provenance detail, veg/non-veg and spice marked on every item, and one consistent house voice.
use_for: menu for a new restaurant, cafe or cloud kitchen
Zomato and Swiggy item descriptions
menu refresh to push high-margin or signature dishes
festive or seasonal special menus (Navratri thali, monsoon specials)
QR or digital menus and tasting menus
avoid: Adjective soup ('delicious, mouth-watering, scrumptious'): says nothing a diner can picture. Name the ingredient, the method and one detail: 'Mutton slow-cooked overnight in a sealed handi with whole spices'.
Exotic house names nobody can order ('The Nawab's Secret') with no explanation. Keep the creative name if the client wants it, but make the description say what it is in the first three words.
Provenance claims the kitchen cannot back ('imported', 'farm-fresh', 'A2 milk'). Use only what the client confirms; misleading claims are an advertising-rules risk.
Use genre:packaging_copy or genre:product_description for packaged food, and genre:hospitality_listing for the restaurant's listing page.

structure.does: Who runs it, what cuisine and region, and the one thing that makes it different, told with a fact.
Clear section names (Starters, Kebabs, Biryani) with an optional one-line intro in house voice.

Main ingredient, cooking method, one sensory or provenance detail; what it comes with if relevant.

checklist: Does every dish name or the first words of its description say what the dish is?
Is every description 25 words or fewer?
Does each description name the main ingredient and the cooking method?
Does each description use at most one generic adjective (tasty, delicious, special)?
Is every item marked veg or non-veg?

Translating regional names into flat English ('Galouti kebab' as 'soft mutton patty'). Keep the original name and explain it once.
Every description in the same rhythm ('X, Y and Z, served with W'). Vary the order across a section.

cards.name: Resume / CV
cards.summary: A one-to-two page record of achievements tuned to one target role, built to parse cleanly in an ATS and to win a fast recruiter skim. Good looks like a headline that matches the target title, a short summary with one or two headline wins, bullets written as action verb + what + measurable result, skills in the job description's own terms, and a plain single-column layout with standard headings.
use_for: job-switch resume for a mid-level professional
fresher or campus resume built from projects and internships
career-change resume that reframes transferable results
senior or executive two-page resume
resume tailored for Gulf, UK or US applications
avoid: Duty lists ('Responsible for vendor management'): they say what the job was, not what the candidate did. Rewrite as result bullets: 'Cut vendor lead time from 21 to 9 days by consolidating 14 suppliers to 6.'

Indian biodata habits (photo, date of birth, marital status, father's name, 'I hereby declare'): not needed for most private-sector jobs and invite bias. Leave them out unless the employer or country asks.
Two-column designer templates with tables, text boxes and icons for key data: many ATS parsers scramble them. Use one column and standard headings.

cards.name: RTI application / citizen grievance letter
cards.summary: A citizen's written request under India's Right to Information Act for specific records held by a public authority, or a formal grievance asking an authority to fix a named problem. Good looks like the right Public Information Officer, one subject, numbered requests for specific records with dates and places, no arguments or allegations, and, for grievances, facts, dates, reference numbers and the remedy sought.
use_for: RTI to a municipal body for contract, measurement and payment records of a public work
RTI on the status of one's own pending file (pension, ration card, land record)
journalist or researcher RTI for data held by a department
first appeal when the reply is late, incomplete or refused
grievance on CPGRAMS or to a department head with a clear remedy
avoid: Questions that ask for opinions or reasons ('Why was my file delayed?'): officers can answer that opinions are not information. Ask for the records that show it: 'Copies of file notings and the movement register for application no. ___ from [date] to [date].'
Ten unrelated subjects in one application: slows the reply and invites partial answers. One subject per application; file separate ones.
Allegations and abuse: they weaken the application and the appeal. State facts and requests only.
Use genre:policy_brief to argue for a change, genre:fact_check to publish what the records show, and genre:scheme_explainer to explain a scheme to citizens.

cards.goal: The officer supplies the exact records within the statutory period, or the applicant has a clean, dated basis for a first appeal (for grievances: the authority acts on the named remedy).

structure.does: The Public Information Officer of the department that holds the records, with office address, or the online portal for that authority.
'Application for information under the Right to Information Act, 2005' plus the topic in a few words.
Name, postal address, phone or email, and a statement that the applicant is a citizen of India.
How the fee was paid under the applicable rules, or the BPL claim with proof attached.
Numbered requests, each for a specific record or data set, with the period, place and reference numbers.
Certified copies, soft copies or inspection of records, as preferred.
Date, place, signature and list of enclosures.
For a grievance: reference numbers, a dated timeline of facts, what was promised versus what happened, the remedy sought and by when, attachments.

length.note: Most RTI applications fit one page; some state rules restrict length, so check the rules of the government concerned. Grievances run longer when a timeline is needed.

checklist: Is it addressed to the PIO of the department that actually holds the records?
Does it cover one subject?
Is each request for a specific record or data set rather than an opinion or a reason?
Does each request give the period, place and any reference numbers?
Is the preferred format (copies, soft copy, inspection) stated?
Is the fee or BPL exemption handled?
Are the applicant's contact details complete?
Is it free of allegations, insults and arguments?
For a grievance: are dates, reference numbers and the remedy sought stated?
pitfalls: Vague periods ('last few years'). Write '1 April 2023 to 31 March 2026'.
Asking a department for records another department holds; the transfer costs time. Find the right authority first (the scheme or works department, not the minister's office).
Asking for personal information about third parties; it is likely to be refused. Ask for aggregate data or records of public work instead.
Mixing a complaint into an RTI ('the officer is corrupt and I demand action'). File the grievance separately; keep the RTI to records.
Not keeping proof of filing (postal receipt, online registration number); the first appeal needs it.
Stiff legal-sounding Hindi copied from templates. Plain, polite Hindi or English is enough.

require.label: asks for records or states a grievance

cards.exemplar_brief: RTI application in Hindi (Devanagari, plain register) from a resident of Ward 14, Gaya (Bihar) to the PIO of Gaya Municipal Corporation asking for the work order, measurement book entries and payment records for a drain built on a named lane between 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026; 150-300 words; numbered requests, no reasons or allegations; goal: the records arrive within 30 days or the applicant can file a first appeal.

Plain Hindi in Bihar's own term (लोक सूचना पदाधिकारी), subject cites section 6(1), citizenship line, three numbered requests each for a specific record (work order, measurement-book pages with date and engineer's signature, bill/voucher/payment records) for 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026, certified-copy format, fee line, section 6(3)/7(1)/10 references correct, no reasons or allegations, 297 words. cards.name: Product onboarding emails (SaaS / app)
cards.summary: Lifecycle emails triggered by what a new user did or did not do, each moving them one step toward the first value moment (activation). Good looks like one action per email, a button that deep-links to the exact screen, a named human sender, under 150 words, and a sequence that stops nudging the moment the user activates.
use_for: free-trial onboarding sequence for B2B SaaS
freemium activation emails for a consumer or fintech app
admin onboarding (connect data, invite team)
re-engaging users who signed up and stalled
trial-ending and trial-to-paid conversion emails

Feature tours listing ten features: users need the next step, not the brochure. One email, one action.
Generic 'Welcome to the family!' openers. Open with the first step and why it matters.

structure.does: Names the activation event, the 2-4 steps before it, and the trigger and exit condition for each email.
Sent on signup. One first step, why it matters, a button to that exact screen, how to get help.
Sent only if the first step is not done. Names the likely blocker and removes it (a 2-minute video, a template, a reply-to-get-help offer).
Sent when the user hits the first value moment. Shows what they got and the next step that deepens use (invite team, connect data).
How a similar customer uses it, with one number and one screenshot description.
What the user has set up, what stops when the trial ends, the recommended plan and price, one button.
Subject plus preheader that say what is inside, a named sender, one primary button, plain layout, a P.S. for help or a reply.

checklist: Does each email state its trigger (did or did not do X) and its exit condition?
Does each email ask for exactly one primary action?
Does the button label name the action (verb + object, e.g. 'Send your first invoice')?
Does each subject line tell the reader what is inside?
Is each email from a named person rather than 'Team'?
Does the button deep-link to the exact screen for the step?
Is each email under 150 words?
Do users who have activated stop receiving nudges?
Do non-transactional emails include unsubscribe or preference options?
Does the trial-end email show what the user built and what they will lose?

The same emails to the admin who bought and the teammate who was invited. Branch by role.
Heavy HTML templates that look like promotions and land in the promotions tab. Keep layout plain with one button.
Three emails on signup day. Space them by behaviour, not by enthusiasm.
A trial-end email that only says 'Your trial ends in 2 days'. Add what they set up, the plan that fits their usage and the price.
Tips about features the user's plan cannot access. Segment by plan before writing.

ban.label: spam and vague link wording

cards.exemplar_brief: Four-email onboarding sequence for a fictional Pune B2B SaaS ('DukaanBooks', GST invoicing for small retailers, 14-day free trial); activation = first GST invoice sent to a customer; email 1 on signup, email 2 only if no invoice within 24 hours, email 3 after the first invoice, email 4 two days before the trial ends; sender: the co-founder; simple Indian English; each email 60-130 words with one button; goal: first invoice sent and trial converted to the Rs 499/month plan.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2-. Activation map with trigger and exit per email, suppression of email 2 once an invoice is sent, a zero-invoice variant for email 4, one action button per email with verb+object labels and deep-link targets, co-founder as sender with reply-to, subjects that say what is inside, 60-130 words each, unsubscribe footer. Email 4 shows what the user built ({invoice_count}, {customer_count}) and the Rs 499 plan. Nits: email 2 switches from 'me' to 'We will help you'; '{invoice_count} invoices' breaks at 1; what stops at trial end is a placeholder.

cards.name: Sales / cold-call script
cards.summary: A call flow for SDRs, telecallers and appointment setters: an honest opener with a reason for calling, three to five discovery questions, a short pitch tied to what the prospect said, answers to the top objections, and a specific next step. Good looks like speech, not prose: short sentences, branches for yes and no, room to listen, and a Hindi or Hinglish version where the callers speak it.
use_for: B2B SDR cold call to book a demo
telecalling script for callbacks to inbound leads (lending, insurance, edtech, real estate, solar)
appointment setting for clinics, salons and site visits
renewal and upsell calls to existing customers
objection-handling sheet for a sales floor
avoid: A two-minute monologue: prospects hang up before the first question. Get to a question within the first 30 seconds.
Misleading openers ('You have won...', 'This is about your account' when it is not): breaks trust and consumer rules. Give the real reason for the call.
Calling numbers without consent or on India's DND registry for promotions: TRAI's TCCCPR rules govern promotional calls. Confirm the lead source and consent with the client before scripting.

Caller name, company, the honest reason for calling tied to the trigger, and a permission check to continue.
Three to five open questions about current situation, problem, impact and timeline; notes on what to listen for.

Top 4-6 objections, each answered acknowledge, ask, answer, and ending with a question.
Asks for a specific next step with two time options, confirms contact details and what happens next.
Short message with the reason and a reply option.

checklist: Does the opener give the caller's name, company and an honest reason within the first two sentences?
Does the caller ask permission before continuing?
Are there at least three open discovery questions?
Does the pitch refer back to something the prospect said?

Does the close ask for a specific time or slot?

Weakness: the subsidy-doubt answer withholds the one public number that ends the doubt (PM Surya Ghar: Rs 30,000/kW for the first 2 kW, Rs 18,000 for the 3rd, capped at Rs 78,000, paid to the bank account). agency credentials ('creds') deck
send-ahead or leave-behind deck read without a presenter
channel, distributor or partner pitch
enterprise proposal presentation

Topic headlines ('Our Solution', 'Features'): they make the reader do the work. Write the takeaway: 'Fleet managers cut idle fuel by a fifth in 60 days.'
Walls of bullets in 12-point type: unreadable on a call. One idea per slide; detail goes to speaker notes or the appendix.

cards.exemplar_brief: 12-slide first-meeting sales deck (headline, body text and speaker notes per slide) for a fictional Gurugram fleet-telematics SaaS ('RahiTrack') selling to logistics companies running 200-2,000 trucks; open with the shift (rising diesel and toll costs), not the company story; one case slide with numbers from a fictional client; end with a 30-day pilot ask; English (Indian); 900-1,400 words in total; goal: the operations head agrees to a pilot. Shift slide: fuel and tolls are about 60% of a long-haul truck's cost per km; a Rs 3 per litre diesel rise adds about Rs 4 crore a year to a 600-truck fleet (each truck burns 22,500 litres a year). Case slide, a fictional 600-truck Gujarat carrier, 90-day pilot on 120 trucks, before to after: idle time 3.4 to 2.3 hours per truck per day (down 32%); fuel 25.0 to 23.7 litres per 100 km (down 5.2%); late deliveries 18% to 11% of trips; a one-line quote attributed only to 'Operations head, fictional carrier'. Good looks like one offer and one big idea carried through every step, each page's headline matching the promise of the click before it, one action per step, and prices, guarantees and deadlines identical everywhere.
use_for: course or workshop funnel (free webinar or masterclass to paid course)
coach or consultant lead-to-call funnel
low-ticket tripwire funnel for a D2C or info product
SaaS lead magnet to demo or trial funnel
5-day challenge funnel
avoid: Writing each page in isolation: the ad promises one thing, the page another, and conversion drops at the gap. Write the funnel map first and repeat the core promise at every step.

Fake scarcity (countdown timers that reset, 'only 3 seats left' that never changes): a dark pattern under India's CCPA guidelines and a trust killer. Use real deadlines and real limits, with the reason.
Income or result promises ('earn Rs 1 lakh a month'): coaching and misleading-ad rules apply. Show typical outcomes with evidence or remove them.
Use genre:sales_page, genre:landing_page, genre:upsell_oto_page and genre:order_form_checkout_copy for the individual pages, and genre:launch_sequence for a time-bound launch.

cards.goal: A visitor moves through every step: opts in, buys the core offer, and a share takes the order bump and upsell, with no step losing them to a mismatched promise.

structure.does: Offer, audience, awareness level, the one promise, each step's single goal and the numbers that must match everywhere (price, guarantee, deadline).
Hook and promise that the opt-in headline will repeat; 2-4 variants.
Headline repeating the ad's promise, 3 bullets on what they get, the form, a privacy line.
Confirms, sets expectations, gives one next micro-step (join the WhatsApp group, watch the 3-minute video, see the starter offer).
Full argument for the core offer (see genre:sales_page).
One-line checkbox offer that complements the core purchase, priced well below it.
The logical next purchase after the core offer, and a smaller alternative if declined.
Separate tracks for buyers (onboarding, upsell) and non-buyers (objections, proof, real deadline).

checklist: Is there a written funnel map naming the offer, audience, awareness level and each step's single goal?
Does each page's headline match the promise of the ad or email that sends people to it?
Does every page have exactly one primary call to action?
Is the order bump relevant to the core purchase and priced well below it?
Does the upsell follow logically from what the buyer just bought without undermining it?
Are deadlines and limits real, with the reason stated?
Are income, health or result claims either substantiated or absent?
Do follow-up emails branch for buyers and non-buyers?
Are prices, guarantee terms and dates identical across every page and email?
Does the opt-in page say how the contact details will be used?
pitfalls: Different prices across steps (Rs 4,999 on the sales page, Rs 5,499 in an email). Keep one numbers sheet and copy from it.
A wasted thank-you page ('Thanks, check your inbox'). It is the highest-intent moment; give the next step.
An upsell that says the core product was incomplete ('the real system is in Pro'). Position the upsell as faster or done-for-you, not as the missing piece.
Insider jargon on cold-traffic pages (funnel, ROAS, 'bump'). Write in the buyer's words.
Hinglish ads leading to stiff English pages. Keep the voice consistent across the journey.
Testimonials with results the funnel cannot back up; use real, permissioned ones with typical outcomes.
cards.exemplar_brief: Funnel copy for a fictional Indore Excel-for-accountants course (Rs 999 core course, Rs 199 order bump for 50 GST templates, Rs 2,999 upsell for a live 4-week batch): one Meta ad, an opt-in page for a free 60-minute workshop, the thank-you page, the sales page's headline, offer stack and FAQ, bump and upsell copy, and 3 follow-up emails; Hinglish (Roman) for the ad and emails, simple English on the pages; 3,000-4,500 words in total; no income claims; goal: workshop sign-ups who go on to buy the course.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. Funnel map with one promise ('stop typing the same figures again every month'), one numbers sheet and a cross-check list; every weekday checks (18 Oct 2026 Sunday, 21 Oct Wednesday, 13 Nov Friday, 16 Nov-9 Dec Mon/Wed = 8 sessions after Diwali); 3 ad variants within Meta limits, opt-in with consent box and data-use line, thank-you page with one micro-step, sales headline/lead/mechanism/offer stack/FAQ, relevant Rs 199 bump, upsell positioned as 'with the trainer' not the missing piece, emails branched for buyers and non-buyers, real deadline with a reason, no income claims. Voice slips: 'aap ... sudhaarte ho' (Ad C) and aap/tum mixing inside the emails ('kholiye' then 'daalte ho', 'dekh sakte ho'); pick one register.

cards.name: Sales page / long-form sales letter
cards.summary: One long page that takes a cold or warm reader from problem to purchase of a single offer. Good looks like a headline that names who it is for and the outcome, a lead that pulls into the body, a mechanism that explains why this works when other attempts failed, proof placed before the price, a clear offer stack with an anchor, a guarantee with plain terms, real objections answered, and every button leading to the same action.
use_for: course, cohort or membership sales page
coaching or consulting programme page that sells a call or an enrolment
D2C hero product long-form page
workshop or event ticket page
SaaS lifetime-deal or annual-plan page
avoid: Superlative stacks ('the most powerful, life-changing programme ever'): readers discount them. Replace each with a specific result, a number or a named testimonial.
Vague benefit bullets ('learn the secrets of success'). Write specific fascinations: 'The 4-line WhatsApp message that gets clients to pay advance without haggling (module 3).'
Fake or stock testimonials and invented 'as seen in' logos: misleading under advertising rules and fatal to trust. Use real, permissioned ones with name, role and result.
Use genre:landing_page for a short single-action page, genre:vsl_script when the sell is a video, and genre:sales_funnel_copy when the client needs the whole funnel.
