cards.goal: The reader buys the offer (or books the call it sells) from this page.

structure.does: Calls out who it is for, states the specific outcome, hints at the mechanism.
A story, a striking fact or the reader's situation in their own words that pulls into the body.
What the problem costs the reader now and if it continues, without exaggeration.
Why common fixes fail and why this approach works; the big idea in one sentence.
The offer named, then specific benefit bullets (fascinations).
Testimonials with names and results, a mini case, credentials; placed before price and near each CTA.
Exactly what the buyer gets, the value of each part, the price and the anchor.
The risk reversal with plain terms and conditions.
The real objections from sales calls and comments, including who it is not for.
Restates the outcome, the offer, the guarantee and any real deadline; final button.

length.note: Price and awareness drive length: a cold reader and a higher price need more argument and proof; a warm list buying a low-price offer needs less.

checklist: Does the headline name who it is for and a specific outcome?
Does the lead get into the reader's situation within the first two sentences?
Is there a mechanism that explains why this works when other attempts failed?
Is every benefit bullet specific (a number, a module, a situation)?
Does proof appear before the price and near each call to action?
Are testimonials real, attributed and permissioned?
Does the offer stack list exactly what the buyer gets, with the price and an anchor?
Are the guarantee terms stated plainly?
Does the FAQ answer real objections, including who the offer is not for?
Does every button lead to the same action?
Is the page free of fake scarcity and unsubstantiated income or health claims?
pitfalls: Throat-clearing leads ('In today's fast-paced world...'). Start in the reader's day: 'It is 11 pm and you are still replying to client WhatsApps.'
Price hidden until the very end with no anchor. Build value first, then show the price against a fair comparison.
Guarantees with conditions buried in the terms page. Put the conditions in the guarantee box.
Walls of text on mobile. Use subheads every few screens, short paragraphs and a button after each major section.
A first-to-market claim in a crowded market (stage-1 promise to a stage-4 reader). Lead with the mechanism or the identity instead.
Health or income results promised to everyone. Describe typical results and the effort involved.

require.label: has a buying call to action

cards.exemplar_brief: Long-form sales page for a fictional Bengaluru nutritionist's 8-week online programme for Indian women with PCOS ('Cycle Reset', Rs 7,999, 30-day refund if the plan is followed and nothing improves in energy or cycle tracking); audience: working women aged 25-38 who have tried crash diets; English (Indian) with occasional Hinglish; 2,500-3,500 words; no cure or weight-loss guarantees; goal: enrolments for the next cohort.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2-. Pre-head calls out the reader, headline names outcome and mechanism, the 4:30 pm crash lead is in her day within two sentences, problem/stakes without exaggeration, one-sentence big idea ('stop dieting at your PCOS and start running it like a routine'), 12-item stack with reasons, Rs 7,999 anchored per week, a real deadline with the reason and a 40-seat cap, refund terms defined plainly (log 5 days a week for 4 weeks; claim by 16 Dec 2026, dates check), FAQ including who it is not for, no cure or weight promise, medical note. Testimonials are permissioned-slot placeholders, correct. Nits: 'Who is this not for' repeats 'speak to your doctor' twice; only one Hinglish touch.

cards.name: Satire / parody piece
cards.summary: Humour that exposes a real target (a politician, a policy, an institution, a trend) through exaggeration, irony or imitation. Good looks like a target with power, a true fact underneath, one absurd premise escalated with strict internal logic, specific details, punchlines at the end of the line, and a clear satire label wherever the piece could pass for real news or an official notice.
use_for: political satire reel or post for a satire page (vyangya)
parody news article or mock press release, clearly labelled
spoof ad mocking a brand or marketing trend
Hindi vyangya column in the Parsai and Sharad Joshi tradition
topical sketch premise for a comedy channel
avoid: Punching down at the poor, minorities, victims, caste or religion: it is cruelty, not satire, and invites legal and platform action. Aim at people and institutions with power and at their actions.
Fabricated quotes or AI voices of real people presented as real: defamation risk and misinformation once screenshots travel. Make the parody frame obvious and label AI-generated likenesses.
Anger with no joke. If the piece has no premise and no punchlines, it is commentary; use genre:political_social_commentary.
Use genre:sketch_comedy for scene-based comedy, genre:meme_caption for one-line meme text, and genre:standup_comedy_set for a stage set.
buyers: political pages and party content cells
comedy channels and creators
digital media outlets with satire sections
brands doing topical humour
cards.value_why: Political pages and comedy channels commission it regularly. Fees track the page's reach and the writer's hit rate rather than word count.
cards.goal: The audience laughs, recognises the real issue underneath, and shares the piece because it says what they think, without anyone mistaking it for real news.

structure.does: Names the target and the real, checkable fact or hypocrisy the piece rests on, with the source link.
One absurd 'what if' that exaggerates the truth ('What if potholes were rebranded as a tourist attraction?').
Builds the world in the target's own register (official notice, news anchor, ad voice) so the absurdity lands.
Three to five beats, each more absurd but following logically from the last.
The line that lands the truth, with the funniest word at the end.
A final callback or button that twists the punchline once more.
A visible 'satire' or 'parody' tag where the format imitates news, official documents or real ads.

length.note: A 30-60 second reel is about 80-150 spoken words; a parody news piece or vyangya column runs 500-1,000. One premise per piece decides the ceiling.

checklist: Is the target a person, institution or trend with power, not a vulnerable group?
Is the underlying fact true and checkable from a named source?
Does a single premise drive the whole piece?
Does each escalation beat follow logically from the one before?
Does each punchline put the funniest word at the end?
Is the piece free of fabricated quotes presented as real?
Is it labelled satire or parody wherever it imitates news, official documents or real ads?
Is it free of slurs and caste or religious insults?
Are AI-generated voices or faces of real people labelled?
Does the length fit the format (reel, post, column)?
pitfalls: Explaining the joke after the punchline. Cut the line after the laugh.
Mocking appearance, accent or family instead of actions and decisions. Target what they did or said.
References only the writer's group gets. Test the premise on someone outside the bubble.
A realistic fake headline screenshot with no label: it travels as news, and the page takes the blame. Put the label inside the image.
Translating English satire into Hindi word for word. Write vyangya natively, with desi idiom and rhythm.
Election-period content that crosses into claims about candidates: check the Model Code and platform rules before posting.
cards.exemplar_brief: Hindi-Hinglish (Roman script) 45-second satirical reel script for a fictional satire page ('Vyang Vaani') about a city's monsoon potholes, written as a deadpan 'official tourism ad' inviting visitors to 'Pothole Adventure Park'; target: the civic administration's repeated pre-monsoon promises, with no private individuals named; 110-150 words of VO plus 4 on-screen text lines and a visible 'satire' label; goal: shares and comments tagging the municipal account, without anyone mistaking it for a real ad.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. Internal target-and-truth with a source slot, one premise (potholes as a tourism attraction) in a deadpan tourism-ad register, three escalating 'rides' (Deep Dive Zone, Free Back Adjustment, Monsoon Mystery Box), the maintenance-by-press-conference beat, punchline 'kaunse monsoon se pehle' and the tag 'Ticket free hai. Aap tax de hi chuke ho.', a persistent SATIRE label, 4 on-screen lines, 137 VO words. Punches up at the civic body; no real person, no invented quote; ribbon-cutter is a stock figure. Slip: 'Aap ... chuke ho' -> 'chuke hain' (aap/ho mismatch).

cards.name: Government scheme explainer (for citizens)
cards.summary: A plain-language explainer that tells citizens who is eligible for a scheme, what they get, which documents they need and how to apply, step by step, with every figure checked against the official guidelines and dated. Good looks like 'am I eligible?' answered first as a checklist, numbered application steps with the official portal, the helpline, an 'as of' date, and the audience's everyday language.
use_for: WhatsApp or Instagram carousel explaining a central or state scheme
reel or YouTube script on how to apply
how-to article or FAQ page for a scheme
pamphlet or booklet for enrolment camps
daily scheme posts for government, party or media content teams
avoid: Figures copied from news reports or forwards: schemes change amounts, limits and dates. Take every number from the official scheme page or guidelines and print the 'as of' date.
Promising the benefit to everyone ('Sabko milega Rs 6,000'). State the conditions and who is excluded.
Political credit-claiming mixed into the eligibility facts. If the brief needs a message, put it in a separate, clearly marked line; keep facts neutral.
Use genre:news_explainer for a policy debate, genre:government_press_note for an official announcement, and genre:public_service_announcement for awareness campaigns.

sources.title: MyGov
sources.supports: platform for citizen-facing scheme communication

buyers: central and state government departments and their agencies
political party content teams
news and explainer media
banks, fintechs, NGOs and CSC operators that help citizens apply
cards.value_why: Government, MyGov, parties and media all produce scheme explainers, and political content teams commission them daily. Steady volume work; value rises with accuracy and regional-language range.
cards.goal: An eligible citizen knows they qualify, gathers the right documents and applies through the official channel, and an ineligible one does not waste a trip.

structure.does: Scheme name, the benefit and who it is for in one line.
Implementing ministry or department and what the scheme gives (cash transfer, subsidy, insurance, loan).
A checklist of conditions, then who is not eligible.
Amounts, form of benefit and when it arrives, exactly as in the official guidelines.
The full list, with plain explanations of terms like e-KYC.
Numbered steps on the official portal or app, plus the offline route (CSC, bank, block office).
How to check status, any deadline, the official helpline and link, the 'as of' date and source.
The usual reasons applications are rejected and how to avoid them.

length.note: A carousel is 8-10 slides and roughly 150-250 words; a reel script 80-150 words; an article or FAQ page 800-1,500 words. The scheme's complexity decides the rest.

checklist: Are the official scheme name and the implementing ministry or department stated?
Is eligibility given as a checklist, including who is not eligible?
Does every amount, limit and date match the official guidelines, with the link and an 'as of' date?
Is the documents list complete?
Are application steps numbered, with the official portal and an offline route?
Is the helpline taken from an official source?
Is the benefit described as conditional on eligibility rather than promised to all?
Is any political message kept separate from the facts?
Is jargon (DBT, e-KYC, seeding) explained in everyday words?
Is it written in the audience's everyday language and register?
pitfalls: Last year's numbers. Re-check the official page on the day of writing; amounts and deadlines change.
Links to look-alike or agent websites: a fraud risk for readers. Link only to the official portal or app.
Sarkari Hindi ('prarupa', 'anupalan sunishchit karein'). Use bolchaal: 'form', 'zaroor karein'.
Dense paragraphs on WhatsApp. One point per line, numbered steps, bold only the scheme name.
Leaving out the offline route; many eligible citizens apply through a CSC or bank, not an app.
During elections, scheme posts from party pages can fall under the Model Code; check before publishing.
cards.exemplar_brief: Hindi (Devanagari, everyday register) 8-slide WhatsApp and Instagram carousel explaining the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana rooftop-solar subsidy for homeowners in Bihar: who is eligible, subsidy by system size, documents, step-by-step application on the official portal, and the helpline; the writer takes every figure from the official scheme portal and prints the 'as of' date; 150-250 words; goal: eligible homeowners start an application on the official portal.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Official name 'PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana' and MNRE, eligibility checklist with an exclusion, subsidy table correct (Rs 30,000 for 1 kW, Rs 60,000 for 2 kW, Rs 78,000 cap at 3 kW and above, to the bank account), documents, numbered portal steps in the right order (register, Bihar discom NBPDCL/SBPDCL, consumer-number login, feasibility approval, registered vendor, net meter, inspection, bank details), offline route via the discom office, helpline 15555, 'as of' date, agent warning, common mistakes; everyday Hindi, 248 words over 8 slides. [verify] tags must be cleared before posting. Hook slide omits the benefit amount ('₹78,000 तक सब्सिडी') that would make it stop the scroll.
